title: Tribal water infrastructure is constrained by eligibility rules, fragmented access, and an underfunded maintenance stage
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office report GAO-26-107178, September 2026

observations.period: Report findings through fiscal year 2026; published September 22, 2026

denominator.unit: GAO evaluation of selected IHS, EPA, and USDA tribal water infrastructure programs

remaining_need.value: IHS estimated that at least $6 billion remained needed as of November 2025 to ensure all tribal communities had safe drinking water and wastewater disposal; GAO reports the residual as $5.3 billion in eligible costs and $1.2 billion in ineligible costs

administrative_burden_example.value: IHS officials reported spending more than 80 hours helping one Tribe obtain an $8,000 grant and additional hours helping report its use
administrative_burden_example.unit: reported staff hours and grant amount for one case

eligibility_boundary.value: IHS eligibility can exclude nontribal homes occupied by tribal members, tribal homes with fewer than five years remaining on a lease, certain community buildings, and new HUD-funded homes

maintenance_capacity.value: As of May 2026, IHS had 22 tribal utility consultants; officials in one area office said four consultants were expected to work with 104 Tribes. IHS generally does not fund routine long-term O&M such as water-operator salaries and energy costs
maintenance_capacity.unit: reported technical-assistance staffing and funding boundary

infrastructure_lifecycle.value: IHS reported eligible costs in its sanitation-deficiency database rising from $4.7 billion in FY2023 to $5.9 billion in FY2024, partly because of aging infrastructure and inadequate operations and maintenance

observations.method: GAO review of agency data and program documents, interagency materials, site visits in Alaska and Arizona, and interviews with Tribes, tribal organizations, and federal officials; the report evaluates eligibility, interagency access, and operations and maintenance.
observations.uncertainty: The report is a program and administrative evaluation, not a population estimate of all tribal water systems or a causal estimate of health effects. The $6 billion need and database-cost figures depend on agency definitions and data quality; the single $8,000 case illustrates burden but is not an average.
observations.subgroup: Tribal communities and the selected IHS, EPA, and USDA programs; findings include examples from Alaska and Arizona and distinguish eligible from ineligible homes and community properties.
observations.counterinterpretation: Fragmentation and maintenance gaps do not mean no infrastructure is delivered or that every eligibility boundary produces harm. Federal agencies and Tribes have collaboration and technical-assistance efforts, and GAO recommends pilots and rule changes rather than claiming that a single funding route would solve all needs.

boundary: This record adds a tribal public-infrastructure access and lifecycle-capacity layer. It does not estimate all tribal health outcomes, assign causal responsibility for infrastructure failure, generalize the illustrative administrative case, or treat proposed GAO recommendations as implemented policy.
